title: Diabetes in pregnancy
blurb: Screen for and diagnose gestational diabetes, apply NICE NG3 glucose targets and treatment steps, plan timing of birth and care for the baby after birth.
question: At booking, Priya has a BMI of 32 and her mother has type 2 diabetes. When should she be offered testing for gestational diabetes, and which test?

teach.body: Formally (NICE NG3): diabetes in pregnancy covers pre-existing type 1 or type 2 diabetes and gestational diabetes (GDM), diagnosed in pregnancy by a fasting plasma glucose of 5.6 mmol/L or above or a 2-hour plasma glucose of 7.8 mmol/L or above on a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT). In plain English: some women arrive with diabetes, others develop it in pregnancy. Both need tight glucose control, because high glucose harms the baby (large baby, birth injury, stillbirth) and causes hypoglycaemia after birth.

teach.h: Who is offered an OGTT for GDM (NG3 1.2.2-1.2.7)?
head: Risk factor at booking
Test
rows: Family origin with high diabetes prevalence
Early self-monitoring or OGTT soon after booking (repeat at 24-28 weeks if normal)
teach.caption: Do not use fasting glucose, random glucose, HbA1c, a glucose challenge test or urine glucose to assess risk of GDM (NG3 1.2.3).

items.label: keep glucose above this if on insulin

teach.caption: NG3 1.2.8, 1.3.5, 1.3.6. Targets apply to all forms of diabetes, if achievable without problematic hypoglycaemia.

children.label: Diet and exercise trial
children.sub: Metformin if targets not met in 1-2 weeks; insulin if still not met

teach.caption: If metformin is contraindicated or unacceptable to the woman, offer insulin.

teach.body: Folic acid 5 mg daily until 12 weeks. Women with type 1 diabetes are offered blood ketone strips and should seek urgent advice if hyperglycaemic or unwell; test urgently for ketonaemia in any woman with diabetes who is unwell, and admit suspected diabetic ketoacidosis immediately to level 2 critical care. Provide glucagon to women with type 1 diabetes. Offer real-time continuous glucose monitoring for type 1. Retinal assessment at booking (unless done in the last 3 months) and at 28 weeks.

teach.caption: Advise women with diabetes to give birth where advanced neonatal resuscitation is available 24 hours a day (1.5.1).

Extra measures (tube feeds or IV dextrose) if glucose is under 2.0 on 2 consecutive readings despite full feeding support, abnormal signs, or not feeding (NG3 1.5.10). Local BAPM-based policies also apply.

teach.h: Scenario: Priya from booking to birth
items: BMI 32 and a mother with type 2 diabetes: two risk factors. The midwife offers a 75 g 2-hour OGTT at 24-28 weeks.
At 26 weeks: fasting 5.9, 2-hour 8.4 mmol/L. GDM is diagnosed and she is seen in the joint clinic within a week.
Fasting under 7.0, so she starts diet and exercise changes; targets are not met after 2 weeks, so metformin is added.
She is advised to give birth no later than 40+6 weeks in a unit with 24-hour neonatal resuscitation.
After the birth: metformin stops immediately; baby feeds within 30 minutes; fasting glucose test for Priya at 6-13 weeks.

teach.text: Don't screen for GDM with urine glucose, random glucose or HbA1c (NG3 1.2.3): the test is a 75 g 2-hour OGTT. And after the birth, women with GDM STOP glucose-lowering treatment immediately, while women with pre-existing insulin-treated diabetes REDUCE their insulin.

items: GDM risk factors: BMI 30 or more, previous baby 4.5 kg+, previous GDM, first-degree relative with diabetes, high-prevalence family origin.
OGTT at 24-28 weeks; diagnose GDM if fasting 5.6+ or 2-hour 7.8+.
Targets: fasting 5.3, 1-hour 7.8 or 2-hour 6.4; above 4 on insulin.
Birth: type 1 or 2 at 37+0 to 38+6; GDM no later than 40+6. Labour glucose 4-7.
Baby: feed within 30 min, glucose at 2-4 h, not home before 24 h. Mother with GDM: fasting glucose at 6-13 weeks, then annual HbA1c.

summary: You can now identify who needs testing for gestational diabetes, interpret OGTT results and glucose targets, and follow the NG3 treatment steps. You can also plan timing of birth, intrapartum glucose control, care of the baby and postnatal follow-up.

A.q: A woman's 75 g OGTT at 26 weeks shows fasting plasma glucose 5.4 mmol/L and 2-hour glucose 8.1 mmol/L. What is the correct interpretation?
A.why: NG3 1.2.8: GDM is diagnosed if fasting is 5.6 or above OR the 2-hour value is 7.8 or above. Either criterion is enough.

whyNot.0: Either value can diagnose GDM; the 2-hour value of 8.1 meets the threshold.
whyNot.2: A diagnostic result does not need repeating before starting care.
whyNot.3: The OGTT result here meets the criteria for gestational diabetes; it does not show pre-existing diabetes.

A.q: At booking, which finding is a risk factor that means a woman should be offered an OGTT for gestational diabetes?
A.why: NG3 1.2.2: a previous macrosomic baby weighing 4.5 kg or more is a risk factor for GDM.

whyNot.1: Maternal age is not one of the NG3 risk factors for GDM.
whyNot.2: Urine glucose should not be used to assess GDM risk (NG3 1.2.3).
whyNot.3: Previous preterm birth is not an NG3 risk factor for GDM.

A.q: A woman with type 1 diabetes asks about her blood glucose targets in pregnancy. What fasting target does NICE NG3 advise?
A.why: NG3 1.3.5: fasting below 5.3 mmol/L, if achievable without problematic hypoglycaemia; women on insulin should stay above 4.

whyNot.0: 6.0 is above the NG3 fasting target.
whyNot.1: 7.0 is the fasting threshold at diagnosis that triggers immediate insulin, not a target.
whyNot.3: Women on insulin should keep glucose above 4 mmol/L, not below it.

B.q: A woman is diagnosed with GDM at 27 weeks. Her fasting glucose was 6.2 mmol/L and there is no macrosomia or polyhydramnios. What is first-line management?
options: Trial of diet and exercise changes
B.why: NG3 1.2.18: fasting under 7.0 at diagnosis: offer a trial of diet and exercise changes first; metformin if targets are not met within 1-2 weeks.

whyNot.0: Immediate insulin is for fasting 7.0 or above, or 6.0-6.9 with macrosomia or polyhydramnios.
whyNot.1: Metformin is offered if targets are not met after 1-2 weeks of diet and exercise.
whyNot.2: The diagnosis is made; repeat testing delays treatment.

B.q: A woman with type 2 diabetes and no complications asks when her baby should be born. What does NICE NG3 advise?
B.why: NG3 1.4.2: elective birth by induction or (if indicated) caesarean between 37+0 and 38+6 weeks for type 1 or type 2 diabetes without complications.

whyNot.1: No later than 40+6 is the advice for gestational diabetes.
whyNot.2: This is later than the NG3 window for pre-existing diabetes.
whyNot.3: Birth before 37 weeks is considered when there are complications, and caesarean is not automatic.

B.q: During labour, a woman with type 1 diabetes has capillary glucose of 8.9 mmol/L. What does NICE advise?
B.why: NG3 1.4.12: use IV dextrose and insulin during labour and birth if capillary glucose is not maintained between 4 and 7 mmol/L.

whyNot.0: Waiting 4 hours leaves glucose above the 4-7 target untreated.
whyNot.1: Stopping fluids does not correct hyperglycaemia and is not the NG3 approach.
whyNot.3: Oral glucose would raise an already high level.

C.q: Baby Ali, born to a mother with GDM, has fed twice. His pre-feed glucose readings are 1.8 and 1.7 mmol/L despite full feeding support. He has no abnormal signs. What does NG3 recommend?
options: Continue feeds and recheck at 24 hours
Use additional measures such as tube feeds
C.why: NG3 1.5.10: use additional measures (tube feeding or IV dextrose) if glucose is below 2.0 mmol/L on 2 consecutive readings despite maximal feeding support.

whyNot.0: Two consecutive readings under 2.0 despite support need escalation, not a long wait.
whyNot.2: Babies of women with diabetes are not transferred home until glucose is stable and they are at least 24 hours old.
whyNot.3: Breastfeeding is supported; the NG3 step is additional measures, not stopping breastfeeding.

C.q: Sunita had GDM treated with metformin. She gave birth this morning. What should happen to her metformin and follow-up?
options: Stop now; fasting glucose at 6-13 weeks
Reduce the dose; HbA1c at 6 weeks
C.why: NG3 1.6.3 and 1.6.11: stop glucose-lowering therapy immediately after birth; offer a fasting plasma glucose test 6-13 weeks after the birth, and do not routinely offer an OGTT.

whyNot.1: Treatment stops at birth, and NICE advises against a routine postnatal OGTT.
whyNot.2: Treatment stops rather than reducing, and fasting glucose is the first-choice test.
whyNot.3: Continuing metformin while breastfeeding applies to women with pre-existing type 2 diabetes, not GDM.

C.q: A woman with type 1 diabetes at 30 weeks phones with vomiting and blood glucose of 16 mmol/L. What should the midwife advise?
options: Stop insulin until she can eat
Book a diabetes clinic next week
Check ketones and seek urgent review
C.why: NG3: test urgently for ketonaemia in a pregnant woman with diabetes who is hyperglycaemic or unwell; suspected DKA needs immediate admission to level 2 critical care.

whyNot.0: Waiting until tomorrow risks missing diabetic ketoacidosis.
whyNot.1: Stopping insulin in type 1 diabetes increases the risk of ketoacidosis.
whyNot.2: A clinic next week is far too slow for possible DKA.

reteach.title: Test, target, time, then baby
reteach.question: Can you walk a woman with GDM from her booking risk assessment to her baby's first day in four steps?

blocks.body: Test: risk factors at booking lead to a 75 g OGTT at 24-28 weeks (earlier if she had GDM before). Target: fasting 5.3, 1-hour 7.8 or 2-hour 6.4, using diet and exercise first, then metformin, then insulin. Time: birth by 40+6 for GDM, 37+0 to 38+6 for type 1 or 2. Baby: feed within 30 minutes, check glucose at 2-4 hours, keep mother and baby together, and stay at least 24 hours.

blocks.text: 5.6 and 7.8 DIAGNOSE GDM; 5.3 and 7.8 (1-hour) are TARGETS. The 7.8 appears in both lists.

explain.body: Risk factors: BMI 30 or more, previous baby 4.5 kg+, previous GDM, first-degree relative with diabetes, high-prevalence family origin. OGTT at 24-28 weeks (early if previous GDM). GDM if fasting 5.6+ or 2-hour 7.8+ (NG3 1.2.2-1.2.8).

test.q: A woman had GDM in her last pregnancy. When should she be offered testing in this pregnancy?
test.why: NG3 1.2.6: previous GDM: offer early self-monitoring or an OGTT as soon as possible after booking, then a further OGTT at 24-28 weeks if the first is normal.

whyNot.0: 24-28 weeks is the standard timing for other risk factors; previous GDM needs earlier testing too.
whyNot.1: 32 weeks is too late and is not an NG3 testing point.
whyNot.2: 36 weeks is far too late to treat and is not an NG3 testing point.

explain.body: Fasting under 7.0: diet and exercise; metformin if targets are not met in 1-2 weeks; insulin if metformin is unsuitable or targets still not met. Fasting 7.0+: immediate insulin with or without metformin.

test.q: A woman with GDM has fasting glucose 7.4 mmol/L at diagnosis. What should be offered?
options: Immediate insulin with or without metformin
test.why: NG3 1.2.22: fasting 7.0 or above at diagnosis: offer immediate insulin, with or without metformin, plus diet and exercise changes.

whyNot.0: A diet trial is for fasting under 7.0 at diagnosis.
whyNot.2: At 7.0 or above, insulin is offered immediately rather than metformin alone.
whyNot.3: The diagnosis is made and treatment should not be delayed.

explain.body: Folic acid 5 mg until 12 weeks; ketone strips and urgent advice if unwell (type 1); glucagon for type 1; retinal assessment at booking and 28 weeks; 20-week scan including the fetal heart; aspirin per NG133.

test.q: A woman with type 1 diabetes is planning a pregnancy. What dose of folic acid should she take?
test.why: NG3 1.1.11: women with diabetes planning a pregnancy take folic acid 5 mg daily until 12 weeks.

whyNot.0: 400 micrograms is the standard dose for women without additional risk factors.
whyNot.2: 10 micrograms is the daily vitamin D dose, not folic acid.
whyNot.3: 1 mg is not the recommended dose.

explain.body: Keep the baby with the mother unless complications need neonatal unit care. Feed within 30 minutes then every 2-3 hours; glucose at 2-4 hours; pre-feed at least 2.0 mmol/L; not home before 24 hours old and until feeding well with stable glucose (NG3 1.5).

test.q: When should the first blood glucose test be done for a well baby of a mother with type 1 diabetes?
test.why: NG3 1.5.3: carry out blood glucose testing routinely at 2 to 4 hours after birth in babies of women with diabetes.

whyNot.0: The first 30 minutes is for the first feed; testing at that point reflects normal early transition.
whyNot.1: 6 hours is later than the NG3 timing.
whyNot.3: Waiting until discharge would miss early hypoglycaemia.
